profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Manasquan Cable Landing Station, tagged here as Apollo, one of the US landing points for the Apollo transatlantic submarine cable system owned and operated by Vodafone Group, a British multinational telecommunications company headquartered in Newbury, Berkshire, England. Apollo provides two geographically diverse fiber optic paths across the Atlantic between the United States and Europe, with a second US landing site in Shirley, New York; its cable segments connect onward to major data center hubs including New York City, Washington DC, and Ashburn, Virginia. This is a distinct facility from the nearby Manasquan TAT-14 cable landing station recorded elsewhere in this registry under the Sprint operator record, since multiple submarine cable systems commonly cluster their US landing points along the same stretch of New Jersey coastline. As a cable landing station rather than a general purpose colocation facility, no critical IT megawattage figure was found or would be expected to be published. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
Manasquan Cable Landing Station (Apollo) is a submarine cable terminus operated by Vodafone on the New Jersey coast, not a data center campus. It is one of two US landing points for the Apollo transatlantic fiber system, which connects onward to major data center hubs in New York City, Washington DC, and Ashburn, Virginia. No IT megawattage capacity is published, as would be expected for a cable landing station rather than a compute facility.

This facility functions as infrastructure for data center connectivity rather than as a host for compute itself. The published megawattage ranking shown in the state context does not apply to this site because it publishes no IT load figure. New Jersey has 48 mapped facilities in the registry, of which only five publish capacity; those five account for 111.3 MW total, but this cable station is not among the sources of that figure.

The site matters to AI infrastructure as a chokepoint for transatlantic data transit to and from major US data center regions, but not as a source of local compute capacity. Its strategic value lies in the submarine cable connectivity it provides to the hubs where AI training clusters are actually deployed. Whether this cable landing station represents a constraint on AI scaling depends on the total available transatlantic fiber bandwidth and utilization, neither of which is published here.
